design_detail: FDG-PET follow-up in the same drug-court programme as Volkow et al. (2001a–c). Five people with methamphetamine dependence scanned after short abstinence (mean 3 months) and again after protracted abstinence (mean 14 months); 8 more scanned once after at least 9 months; cross-sectional comparison with 11 non-using controls and with the 12 users scanned in short abstinence. Motor, memory and attention tests repeated in the 5 retested users only.
can_establish: That in the 5 retested users relative thalamic metabolism rose between scans while striatal metabolism did not change, and that striatal metabolism was lower than in controls in both short- and protracted-abstinence groups.
cannot_establish: That thalamic metabolism 'recovers' in people who stop using generally (5 selected completers; test statistics internally inconsistent); that thalamic change produced the test improvements (5 people, no retested controls for practice effects); or anything about amotivation or anhedonia (not measured).

sample.recruitment: Users enrolled in a California drug-court monitoring rehabilitation programme with weekly or biweekly drug screens and daily centre visits; controls by advertisement (p. 243).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence; average use at least 0.25 g/day, 5 days a week, 2 years; at least 2 weeks' abstinence. Excluded: HIV seropositivity, comorbid neuropsychiatric disorder, medical illness, dependence on other drugs except nicotine (p. 243).
sample.demographics: Retested users: 3 women, 2 men, age 29 (SD 3). Users tested once: 6 women, 2 men, age 36 (SD 3). Controls: 7 women, 4 men, age 31 (SD 7). Short-abstinence group of 12: 7 women, 5 men, age 30 (SD 6) (p. 243). Education, IQ and smoking not reported.
sample.attrition: Of 12 users first scanned within 6 months of last use, only 5 stayed drug-free for 9 months and were rescanned; relapsers were excluded from follow-up (pp. 243, 247).
sample.selection_effects: The retested users are those who stayed abstinent, a group shown in the companion DAT paper to have had higher baseline DAT and better test scores than dropouts (Volkow et al., 2001b, p. 9416). In this programme relapse meant a return to jail (p. 247).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported history; random urine screens within 2-week periods plus a pre-scan urine test (pp. 243, 247).
exposure.polysubstance: Dependence on other drugs except nicotine excluded; other use not quantified.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Retested: 3 months (SD 1.6) then 14 months (SD 2), i.e. 12–17 months. Once-only: 17 months (SD 10). Short-abstinence group: 64 days (SD 40) (pp. 242–243). The authors note intermittent use between random tests could have been missed (p. 247).

comparison.controls: 11 non-using volunteers recruited by advertisement, scanned once (p. 243).
comparison.matching: Described as age-matched; sex mix similar; education, IQ and smoking not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Excluded for drug abuse or dependence other than nicotine (p. 243).

outcomes.instruments: FDG-PET at rest; striatum, thalamus and occipital cortex (control region) by template regions of interest; relative measures = region/global; SPM99 (p. 243). Timed Gait, Grooved Pegboard, Rey AVLT (immediate, delayed, interference recall), Symbol Digit Modalities Test in users only (p. 243).
outcomes.validity_norms: Test scores were compared neither with controls nor with norms.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Recovery' = within-person change in relative metabolism; 'functional significance' = correlation of metabolic change with test-score change in 5 people.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None for region-of-interest or correlation analyses; the authors say they limited the number of tests to avoid multiple comparisons (p. 247). SPM: voxel p<0.001 with cluster-level correction (p. 243).

analysis.effect_sizes: Retested users, short vs protracted: no change in global (42.6 vs 40.8 µmol/100 g/min) or absolute regional metabolism; relative thalamic metabolism +12% (SD 9%), reported as t=2.3, df=9, p<0.05; striatum +2.7% (SD 6.7%), occipital +0.4%, not significant (p. 244). Correlations of thalamic change with test change in the 5: Timed Gait r=0.88, Symbol Digit r=0.96, delayed recall r=0.98 (each df=3); Grooved Pegboard r=0.26 and immediate/interference recall r=0.32 not significant (p. 244; Figure 2, p. 245). Cross-sectional: relative caudate metabolism lower than controls (1.35, SD 0.06) after short (1.20, SD 0.10) and protracted abstinence (1.23, SD 0.09); putamen likewise; thalamus lower after short abstinence (1.11 vs 1.31, t=−5.3) but 'not different' after protracted abstinence (1.23 vs 1.31) (p. 244). Editors' calculation from the reported means and SDs: protracted-abstinence thalamus vs controls d≈−0.8, p≈0.05–0.07, so the thalamus did not return to control levels in any demonstrated sense. Users after protracted abstinence had higher thalamic metabolism than users after short abstinence (t=−3.8, df=23) with no striatal difference (p. 245).
analysis.selective_reporting: Test scores are reported only as correlations with metabolic change; their raw changes and practice effects are not reported.
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors note the small, possibly unrepresentative sample (p. 247).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 5 selected abstinent users, relative thalamic metabolism rose and striatal metabolism did not; striatal metabolism stayed below controls in short and protracted abstinence; within the 5, larger thalamic increases went with larger test-score gains on 3 of 5 measures.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and discussion present thalamic 'recovery' as associated with improved motor and memory performance and therefore functionally significant (abstract; pp. 245–247), and suggest that lower accumbens metabolism could account for persistent amotivation and anhedonia (abstract; p. 246), which the study did not measure. The summary speaks of protracted abstinence and rehabilitation reversing some methamphetamine-induced alterations (p. 247), a causal reading the design cannot support. The test 'improvements' have no practice-effect control.

timeline.event: Baseline metabolism study of the original 12-plus users
DAT follow-up of the same 5 retested users
Critical review: no educational data, no normative comparison of cognitive scores
Review: thalamic change correlated with test improvement, but no procedure controlled for practice effects

replication.where_it_stands: A control-retested FDG study over the first month of abstinence (10 users, 12 controls) found larger increases in global metabolism in users than in controls (Berman et al., summarized by Dean et al., 2013, p. 265); no study has repeated the 12-month thalamic finding.

funding.funder: US Department of Energy contract; National Institute on Drug Abuse grants; Office of National Drug Control Policy; NIH General Clinical Research Center grants (p. 247).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Same group and programme as Volkow et al. (2001a–c).

what_would_settle_it: Repeated imaging and testing over 12–24 months in all people entering treatment, including those who relapse, with non-using controls retested at the same intervals.

domains.note: Smoking, education and other drug use not reported or adjusted.
Abstinence monitored by random urine screens; intermittent use possible (p. 247).
Only those who stayed abstinent were followed; relapsers excluded.
Daily programme attendance, cognitive behaviour therapy, threat of jail.
No retested controls for metabolic test–retest variation or practice effects on tests.
Group composition for the control comparison differs between methods and results; test outcomes reported only as correlations.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A 5-person selected follow-up with inconsistent statistics; the cross-sectional comparisons share the confounding of the parent study.

key_findings.finding: In 5 users rescanned at 12–17 months, relative (region-to-global) thalamic metabolism rose by 12% (SD 9%), while relative striatal (+2.7%) and occipital (+0.4%) metabolism showed no significant change; global metabolism (42.6 vs 40.8 µmol/100 g/min) and absolute regional metabolism, including the thalamus, did not change significantly.
key_findings.note: Reported as t=2.3, df=9; a paired test in 5 people has df=4 (p≈0.08 for t=2.3); the reported mean and SD imply t≈3.0, p≈0.04 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Relative caudate and putamen metabolism were lower than in controls both after short and after protracted abstinence.
Relative thalamic metabolism was lower than controls after short abstinence (1.11 vs 1.31) and described as not different after protracted abstinence (1.23 vs 1.31).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: d≈−0.8, p≈0.05–0.07; not evidence of return to control levels.

key_findings.finding: In the 5, thalamic change correlated with change on Timed Gait (r=0.88), Symbol Digit (r=0.96) and delayed recall (r=0.98), not with pegboard or immediate recall.
key_findings.note: The direction of these correlations is uncertain: read against the same five people's mean test scores in Volkow et al. (2001b, pp. 9415–9416), the plotted changes imply that larger thalamic increases went with smaller improvements (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Neuropsychological tests were given to users only and limited to tests previously correlated with DAT.
Relapse in the programme meant a return to jail; urine tests were random within 2-week windows.
Absolute global metabolism did not differ significantly between the 11 controls (33.8, SD 7.4 µmol/100 g/min) and users after short (38.5, SD 8.5) or protracted abstinence (37.3, SD 6.3).
key_findings.note: The short-abstinence users are those of Volkow et al. (2001c), whose 14% global elevation was reported against a different control group of 21; the comparisons share participants and are not independent. Editors' calculation, short abstinence vs controls: d≈0.6 (95% CI about −0.25 to 1.42).

reporting_issues.issue: The paired comparison in 5 people is reported with df=9 (expected 4), and the test statistics do not match the reported means and SDs of the change: thalamus +12% (SD 9%) implies t≈3.0, not 2.3; striatum +2.7% (SD 6.7%) implies t≈0.9 with 5 people (the printed t=1.3 would need about 10 observations); occipital +0.4% (SD 9%) implies t≈0.1, not 1.2.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline thalamic increase is borderline (p between about 0.04 and 0.08 depending on which reported number is right) and rests on 5 people.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods say the comparison with controls used 10 protracted-abstinence users (the 5 retested plus 5 of the 8 tested once), but the reported degrees of freedom (df=22 with 11 controls) imply 13, and a later comparison uses N=13; why 3 users were left out, or whether they were, is not explained. The short-abstinence group is likewise described as the 7 users who did not stay abstinent (Introduction; Method, Subjects, p. 243) but analysed as the original 12 (Statistical Analysis; df=21), which include the 5 retested, so the unpaired short- versus protracted-abstinence comparison (12 vs 13, df=23, p. 245) counts the same 5 people in both groups.
Amotivation and anhedonia are discussed as consequences of lower accumbens metabolism (abstract; p. 246) but were not measured.
reporting_issues.consequence: Speculation appears in the abstract's conclusions.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 2 does not state the sign convention of its score changes, and they cannot be reconciled with the means reported for the same five people in Volkow et al. (2001b): there Timed Gait went from 10.0 to 8.6 s and delayed recall from 11.6 to 12.8 words, whereas the plotted changes average about +13% for Timed Gait and about −12% for delayed recall (editors' reading of the points).
reporting_issues.consequence: If the plotted values are earlier-minus-later changes (the reading consistent with Volkow et al., 2001b), the three significant correlations run opposite to the abstract: larger thalamic increases went with smaller improvements. If they are later-minus-earlier, most of the five got slower and recalled fewer words. Either way the abstract's link to improved performance is not supported as stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The tests are said to be those previously shown to correlate with DAT, but the Symbol Digit Modalities Test did not correlate with DAT in Volkow et al. (2001a, pp. 379–380) and was not among the tests retested in Volkow et al. (2001b).
reporting_issues.consequence: The stated basis for choosing the tests does not hold for one of the three tests that produced a significant correlation.

reporting_issues.issue: The nucleus accumbens decrease after protracted abstinence, which the abstract highlights, is reported only in the text from statistical parametric mapping; Figure 3 shows the short-abstinence comparison only, and no cluster size, coordinates or statistics are given for the protracted group.
reporting_issues.consequence: The accumbens finding after protracted abstinence, and the amotivation and anhedonia interpretation built on it, cannot be checked from the paper.

disagreements.first_pass: In 5 users rescanned at 12–17 months, relative thalamic metabolism rose by 12% (SD 9%) while striatal (+2.7%) and occipital (+0.4%) metabolism did not change; global metabolism unchanged.
disagreements.reviewer: Confirmed; 'did not change' for striatum and occipital cortex is better as 'no significant change'. Missed: the thalamic increase is in relative values only; absolute thalamic metabolism did not change significantly and global metabolism fell from 42.6 to 40.8 (p. 244).
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on p. 244 (Results, 1st paragraph). Wording made exact and the relative-only nature of the thalamic increase stated in the finding itself; note on the test statistics kept.

disagreements.reviewer: Confirmed; values match the Figure 2 footnotes (p. 245); the Timed Gait relation is plotted with a negative slope while r is printed unsigned; see missed for a sign problem in this figure.
disagreements.resolution: Added a note pointing to the new reporting issue on Figure 2, so that a claim citing this finding carries the caveat.

disagreements.first_pass: The paired comparison in 5 people is reported with df=9 (expected 4), and the t values do not match the reported mean and SD of the change (12%, SD 9% implies t≈3.0, not 2.3).
disagreements.reviewer: Confirmed; extend to the other two regions (striatum t=1.3 fits 10 observations; occipital t=1.2 is impossible from the printed mean and SD).
disagreements.resolution: Recomputed all three: thalamus t=2.98 (n=5); striatum t=0.90 (n=5) or 1.27 (n=10); occipital t=0.10 (n=5). Issue extended to the three regions.

disagreements.first_pass: The methods say the comparison with controls used 10 protracted-abstinence users (the 5 retested plus 5 of the 8 tested once), but the reported degrees of freedom (df=22 with 11 controls) imply 13, and a later comparison uses N=13; why 3 users were left out, or whether they were, is not explained.
disagreements.reviewer: Confirmed; also the short-abstinence group: described as the 7 non-completers (p. 243) but analysed as the original 12 (df=21), which include the 5 retested; the short-vs-protracted unpaired test (12 vs 13, df=23, p. 245) therefore counts the same 5 people in both groups.

Missed: cross-sectional global metabolism in users (short 38.5, protracted 37.3) was not significantly higher than in these 11 controls (33.8) (p. 244); the 12 short-abstinence users are the same people who, in Volkow 2001c, were 14% above 21 controls; d≈0.6 (95% CI −0.25 to 1.42).
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on p. 244; d and interval recomputed from the printed means and SDs (pooled SD 8.0; d=0.59). Added as a key finding because it bears on the glucose-metabolism claim.

disagreements.reviewer: Missed: the score changes in Figure 2 cannot be reconciled with the means reported for the same five people in Volkow 2001b (Timed Gait 10.0 to 8.6 s; delayed recall 11.6 to 12.8 words); read as earlier-minus-later, all three significant correlations run the other way.
disagreements.resolution: Checked on a 400-dpi crop of Figure 2 (p. 245): the plotted points reproduce the printed r values (my values −0.88, 0.97, 0.98) and their mean changes are about +13% (Timed Gait), −13% (Symbol Digit) and −12% (delayed recall); the companion means are on Volkow 2001b pp. 9415–9416. No sign convention reconciles both. Added as a reporting issue.

disagreements.reviewer: Missed: the stated rationale that the tests were those previously correlated with DAT (pp. 243, 247) does not fit the Symbol Digit Modalities Test.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed against Volkow 2001a (only Trail Making approached significance among the exploratory tests, p. 380) and Volkow 2001b (retested Timed Gait, Pegboard and AVLT only, p. 9415). Added.

disagreements.reviewer: Missed: the SPM figure shows only short abstinence vs controls (Figure 3, p. 246); the protracted-abstinence SPM results (nucleus accumbens decreases) are described but not shown.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed (text p. 244; Figure 3 title and note, p. 246). Added.
